The public key creates the signature, the private key verifies
The private key creates the signature, the public key verifies
A single derived HMAC key is used for both signing and verifying

/.env, a file that also leaks the matching RSA private key
/jwks.json, the JSON Web Key Set document for verification keys
/public.pem, a raw PEM file served from the web root directly
questions.x: /jwks.json is a standard JSON Web Key Set endpoint. Publishing the public key is normal for RS256, but that same material becomes the HMAC secret in this attack.
questions.h: The lab says the public key is on a standard endpoint. The filename abbreviates JSON Web Key Set.

questions.q: Why is publishing the RSA public key safe under correct RS256 verification?
o: The key is encrypted with a passphrase before it is published
The public key cannot produce a valid RS256 signature by itself
The published key expires after a short, server-defined window
The public key is a hash of the RSA material, not the real key
questions.x: Creating an RS256 signature requires the private key. The public key only verifies. Downloading it does not let an attacker sign new tokens while the server still enforces RS256.
questions.h: Which RSA operation needs the private key, and which one only needs the public key?

questions.q: What is the root flaw exploited by algorithm confusion in this lab?
o: The RSA key pair is too short to resist a practical brute-force
The server trusts the token's alg header instead of its own config
The JWKS endpoint accidentally publishes the RSA private key too
RS256 has a known break in the SHA-256 hashing step of the signature
questions.x: A vulnerable verifier reads alg from the attacker-controlled header and switches logic. Setting alg to HS256 puts the server in HMAC mode, where the public key is treated as the secret.
questions.h: The attacker controls the JWT header. Which header field can change which algorithm the server uses to verify?

questions.q: In this attack, what value is used as the HS256 HMAC secret?
o: An empty string read from /dev/null after a kid path traversal
The server's RSA public key material, converted to PEM, as HMAC
A randomly generated 256-bit key created only on the attacker side
The original JWT signature bytes reused as the new HMAC secret
questions.x: The public key is fetched from /jwks.json and converted to PEM. The attacker HMACs with those PEM bytes. A confused server verifies the HS256 token with the same public key material.
questions.h: If the server verifies HS256 using its own public key, what must the attacker use as the HMAC secret when signing?

PEM format, with a BEGIN PUBLIC KEY header wrapping the key

The raw JWKS JSON object string used directly as the HMAC secret

questions.h: The usual text form for an RSA public key starts with a BEGIN PUBLIC KEY line.

Changing the sub claim to administrator before signing HS256

questions.q: Which of the following is true of this lab's algorithm confusion attack?
o: The public key at /jwks.json is enough to forge a valid RS256 token
The attack keeps alg as RS256 and only edits the payload sub claim
None of these statements are true about this algorithm confusion lab
The HMAC secret is an empty string read from /dev/null on disk
questions.x: A public key cannot forge RS256. The attack switches alg to HS256 and HMACs with the PEM public key. Empty-string /dev/null signing is the kid lab, not this one.
questions.h: Separate RS256 forgery, the actual alg switch, and the /dev/null trick from the kid lab.

questions.q: What server-side change fully prevents algorithm confusion on this verifier?
o: Rotate the RSA key pair more frequently without changing the code
Enforce the expected algorithm from config and reject any other alg
Restrict /jwks.json to authenticated users so the key stays hidden
Use 4096-bit RSA instead of 2048-bit without pinning the algorithm
